findings.title: Method name typo 'santizeAnchors' instead of 'sanitizeAnchors'
findings.body: The new method is named `santizeAnchors`, missing the 'i'. This typo will propagate to any logs, error messages, or future callers, and makes the code harder to maintain. It should be `sanitizeAnchors`.

findings.title: Narrow literal removal of '<!-- -->' may miss sanitizer variants
findings.body: The code unconditionally does `sanitized = sanitized.replace("<!-- -->", "");` to strip the comment separator that the OWASP sanitizer inserts between adjacent text blocks. However, the sanitizer emits comments with varying internal whitespace (e.g. `<!--  -->`, `<!--->`), so this literal replacement leaves artifacts behind. As a result, when the sanitizer splits adjacent text blocks the verifier can still register a spurious difference and incorrectly flag the translation as containing illegal HTML. A regex such as `<!--\s*-->` should be used.

findings.title: IOException from missing English counterpart is wrapped as RuntimeException
findings.body: In `verifySafeHtml`, when the English counterpart file cannot be opened, the IOException is caught and rethrown as `new RuntimeException("unable to read file " + englishFile, e)`. The other I/O failure paths in the class surface errors via `MojoExecutionException` (declared on the public `verify` method) so this RuntimeException is inconsistent and bypasses the standard failure reporting of the Maven plugin. Additionally, if a translation is added before its English source lands (e.g. a brand-new locale) the verification will crash instead of skipping or warning. There is also no test for this scenario.

findings.title: English-file path derivation uses a regex that can map unrelated locales to _en
findings.body: The expression `file.getAbsolutePath().replaceAll("resources-community", "resources").replaceAll("_[a-zA-Z-_]*\\.properties", "_en.properties")` matches any underscore-prefixed locale segment (the inner character class includes `-` and `_` so the suffix can contain hyphens too). It will therefore map, for instance, `messages_zh_TW.properties` to `messages_en.properties` instead of `messages_zh_Hant.properties`/etc., and will silently turn `messages_.properties` into `messages_en.properties`. There is no test that asserts the English counterpart is selected correctly for non-`_en` locales.

findings.title: HTML_TAGS regex only matches lowercase HTML tags
findings.body:
`Pattern HTML_TAGS = Pattern.compile("<[a-z]+[^>]*>")` only matches tags whose name begins with one or more ASCII lowercase letters, so `containsHtml` returns false for tags such as `
`, `

`, `
`, or attributes-only constructs. When the English source happens to use uppercase tags, POLICY_NO_HTML is incorrectly selected and the OWASP sanitizer is then forced to make a structural decision that POLICY_SOME_HTML was meant to handle, producing false positives. Case-insensitive matching (`(?i)<[a-z]+[^>]*>`) or explicit handling of uppercase letters is needed.

findings.title: Anchor sanitizer can incorrectly flag repeated/misordered anchors
findings.body: In `santizeAnchors` the local `Matcher matcher` is created from the original `value`, while the loop also reassigns `value = value.replaceFirst(Pattern.quote(englishMatcher.group()), "")`. The Matcher still searches the unstripped original, but its `find()` advancement combined with `englishMatcher.find()` advancement causes two false-positive scenarios: 1. If the translation legitimately repeats the same anchor (e.g. `link ... link`) while English has only one, the second translation anchor finds no remaining English anchor and the method reports "Didn't find anchor tag ... in original string" even though no malicious anchor was added. 2. If a translation reorders two anchors relative to English, the first match succeeds and removes the first anchor from `value`, then the second translation anchor is compared against the (now second) English anchor and is flagged as missing. Both cases will be reported as illegal anchor use even when the resulting sanitized HTML is identical to the English source. The matcher state should be re-derived from the modified `value` after each successful replacement, or the comparison should be done on the anchor sets rather than positionally.

findings.title: No test coverage for missing English source file
findings.body: There is no test that exercises the case where a translation file's English counterpart is absent or unreadable. `verifySafeHtml` will throw a `RuntimeException` (wrapping a `FileNotFoundException`) in that case, crashing the whole verification rather than reporting a clean error. A regression test calling `verify()` on a translation whose derived `_en` path does not exist should be added and the method should translate the IOException into `MojoExecutionException` to match the rest of the class.

findings.title: No test exercises the new anchor path on real translations
findings.body: The anchor sanitizer is the only defense against a translator pointing an existing English anchor at a malicious URL (the test fixture does cover that), but there is no test that verifies the case where a translation uses the same anchor as English and is therefore silently stripped without error. Likewise there is no test for the `<0>...</0>`/`<1>...</1>` style parameterized placeholders that many `messages_*.properties` files use (e.g. `resourceSharedWith_one`). Because `HTML_TAGS` does not match `<0>` etc., the verifier will select POLICY_NO_HTML for those values, and the OWASP sanitizer (which treats `<0>` as an unknown tag) will strip them, causing the verifier to flag legitimate translations as illegal HTML. This should be tested explicitly and either the policy decision or the normalize step needs to handle `<n>` placeholders.
